title: ML and AI for density functional theory: different priorities for Kohn-Sham and orbital-free DFT, for electronic and nuclear DFT
abstract: We overview similarities and, importantly, differences in computational bottlenecks and accuracy requirements that can be addressed with machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI) techniques in electronic and nuclear DFT. From these follow different promising methodological and algorithmic choices depending on whether one machine learns the exchange correlation (XC) functional, the kinetic energy functional (KEF), the density or the basis functions. In particular, while the popular deep neural networks remain a potent choice in the context of KS DFT, we highlight their disadvantages when building KEFs and highlight conceptual advantages - yet to be fully realized - of symbolic regression for both electronic and nuclear DFT. We point out promising approaches that can be carried from the more extensively investigated ML-enhanced electronic DFT to nuclear DFT.
summary: This review surveys how Machine Learning and AI can revolutionize Density Functional Theory (DFT) for both electronic and nuclear structure calculations. It critically distinguishes between applying ML to the exchange-correlation functional versus approximating kinetic energy functionals directly from density. The work highlights that different physical regimes require tailored algorithmic approaches, suggesting a path forward for computationally intensive quantum simulations.
main_problem: The paper addresses computational bottlenecks and accuracy requirements when applying Density Functional Theory (DFT) to both electronic and nuclear systems.
main_result: It outlines distinct methodological pathways for incorporating Machine Learning (ML) and Artificial Intelligence (AI), distinguishing between improving the exchange-correlation functional, kinetic energy functional, or basis sets.
method: The authors compare standard DFT approaches (Kohn-Sham vs. Orbital-Free) with ML techniques like deep neural networks and symbolic regression to accelerate calculations.
model_or_system: The scope covers electronic systems (atoms, molecules) governed by the Schrödinger equation in a mean-field approximation, and nuclear systems involving nucleons interacting via the strong force. Both are treated using density functionals ($ho$).
key_observables: Electronic energies, band structures, binding energies, radii, and equations of state for nuclear matter.
important_parameters: The dimensionality of the problem (high), the scaling cost of standard methods (e.g., cubic scaling in KS DFT), and the specific functional being approximated (XC or KEF).
main_assumptions: DFT is used to reduce N-body problems to density functionals; ML/AI must address different quantitative needs for electronic vs. nuclear systems.
paper_structure: The paper provides an overview, first detailing the computational challenges in both electronic and nuclear DFT, then mapping out how ML/AI can target specific components (XC functional, KEF) with different algorithmic choices.
why_interesting: While focused on condensed matter/nuclear physics, the core theme of using advanced machine learning techniques to solve high-dimensional many-body equations is highly relevant to developing efficient quantum simulation methods.
